key_terms.meaning: α = (10/L)·log₁₀(P_in/P_out) in dB/km, where L is length in km and P_in, P_out are optical powers in the same unit.
A power ratio expressed as 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁); 3 dB means half the power, 10 dB means one tenth.
Low-loss bands near 850 nm, 1310 nm and 1550 nm; single-mode silica gives about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm.
Absorption by the SiO₂ network itself: an ultraviolet edge below about 0.4 μm and an infrared tail beyond about 1.6 μm.
Absorption by impurities: OH⁻ ions peak near 950 nm, 1240 nm and 1380 nm, and metal ions add a broad background loss.
α_R = C/λ⁴ with C ≈ 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·μm⁴ for silica, giving about 0.15 dB/km at 1550 nm.
Scattering from defects whose size is comparable to the wavelength; it varies slowly with λ and is cut by clean fabrication.
Extra loss when the whole fiber is curved to a radius of a few millimetres or less.
Loss from tiny random kinks along the fiber axis, caused by coating, cabling or temperature stress.
R_c ≈ 3n₁²λ / (4π(n₁² − n₂²)^{3/2}); below this radius the bend loss rises exponentially.
Pulse spread from different mode path lengths; for step index ΔT/L ≈ n₁Δ/c with Δ = (n₁ − n₂)/n₁.
Core index falls as n(r) = n₁√(1 − 2Δ(r/a)^α); with α ≈ 2 the spread falls to ΔT/L ≈ n₁Δ²/(8c).
D_m = −(λ/c)·d²n/dλ² in ps/(nm·km); it is zero for silica near 1270 nm.
Change of the mode propagation constant with wavelength caused by the core–cladding geometry; its value is negative in the 1550 nm band.
D = D_m + D_w in ps/(nm·km); about +17 ps/(nm·km) for standard single-mode fiber at 1550 nm.
Random delay between the two polarization modes; the mean differential group delay grows as the PMD coefficient times √L, in ps.
Fiber whose index profile is redesigned so that total dispersion is zero at 1550 nm instead of near 1310 nm.
A short fiber with large negative D, about −100 ps/(nm·km), placed to cancel the positive dispersion of the link.
Above a threshold of a few milliwatts, light is scattered backward with a shift of about 11 GHz at 1550 nm.
Forward scattering with a shift of about 13 THz; its threshold is far above the SBS threshold, and the gain is used in Raman amplifiers.

takeaways: Attenuation sets the reach of a link, and in silica it is quoted as a coefficient in dB/km rather than as a plain ratio.
Intrinsic absorption is a property of the glass itself, while extrinsic absorption comes from impurities such as OH⁻ and metal ions.
Rayleigh scattering falls as 1/λ⁴ and is the physical reason the 1550 nm window is the lowest-loss window.
Bending loss is negligible until the bend radius approaches a critical value, then it grows exponentially with further tightening.
In a multimode fiber the pulse spread is set by path-length differences between modes, and grading the core cuts it by roughly a factor of Δ/8.
In a single-mode fiber the spread comes from chromatic dispersion, the sum of a material part and a waveguide part.
Standard single-mode fiber has its zero-dispersion wavelength near 1310 nm, so a 1550 nm link needs dispersion management.
Polarization mode dispersion is random and grows as √L, so it matters for long, high-bit-rate links rather than short ones.
Dispersion-shifted and dispersion-compensating fibers treat dispersion as a design choice rather than a fixed property.
Nonlinear scattering puts a ceiling on launched power, since beyond a threshold the signal pumps a scattered wave and loses power.
bank_note: Long answers are expected to combine a labelled loss-versus-wavelength curve with the numbers 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, the OH⁻ peaks, the 1/λ⁴ Rayleigh law and the 1310 nm versus 1550 nm dispersion trade-off, then move on to dispersion types and their units.

bank.q: Define the attenuation coefficient of an optical fiber. Derive its expression in dB/km and explain why loss is quoted this way.
outline: State α = (10/L)log₁₀(P_in/P_out) with L in km and both powers in the same unit.
Show the step from the natural logarithm form to the base-10 decibel form.
Explain that the coefficient is per kilometre, so link loss is αL, and that it allows simple addition of fiber, splice and connector losses.
Give typical values: about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm, 2 to 3 dB/km at 850 nm.

bank.q: Distinguish intrinsic and extrinsic absorption in silica glass fibers and name the wavelengths where each is serious.
outline: Intrinsic: electronic absorption in the ultraviolet below about 0.4 μm and vibrational absorption in the infrared beyond about 1.6 μm; both tails reach into the usable window.
Extrinsic: OH⁻ ion peaks near 950 nm, 1240 nm and 1380 nm, the last being the strongest.
Metal ion impurities such as Fe, Cu, Cr, Mn add broadband loss.
Removal by purification and by drying the preform, giving low-water-peak fiber.
Both together set part of the loss floor of the fiber alongside Rayleigh scattering.

bank.q: Explain Rayleigh scattering in an optical fiber and show why its loss falls as 1/λ⁴.
outline: Origin: density and composition fluctuations frozen into the glass during drawing, on a scale much smaller than the wavelength.
Each fluctuation acts as a tiny dipole scatterer; scattered power follows the λ⁻⁴ law of Rayleigh scattering.
Write α_R = C/λ⁴, C ≈ 0.8 dB·km⁻¹·μm⁴ for silica; at 1.55 μm this is about 0.15 dB/km.
It is the dominant loss mechanism in modern fiber between about 1.3 μm and 1.6 μm and cannot be removed, only reduced by longer wavelength.
Compare with Mie scattering from larger defects, which is flatter in wavelength and is reduced by better fabrication.

bank.q: Explain bending losses in optical fibers. Distinguish macrobending from microbending and state what happens as the bend radius is reduced.
outline: Macrobending: a visible curve of a few millimetres radius or less.
Microbending: random microscopic kinks along the axis from coating, cabling or thermal stress.
Physical cause: on the outside of the bend the field must travel faster than the plane wave in the cladding, so the tail beyond the caustic radiates away.
Loss stays tiny above a critical radius R_c ≈ 3n₁²λ/(4π(n₁² − n₂²)^{3/2}) and then rises exponentially as R falls below it.
Longer wavelength and smaller Δ both make bending loss worse; single-mode fiber in the 1550 nm band is the most sensitive.

bank.q: Define intermodal dispersion and chromatic dispersion and state the units in which each is measured.
outline: Intermodal: different modes have different path lengths, so one pulse splits into a train of arrivals; spread is proportional to length, in ns or ps per km.
Chromatic: within one mode, different wavelengths travel at different group velocities; measured as D in ps/(nm·km).
Chromatic = material dispersion plus waveguide dispersion.
Intermodal dispersion exists only in multimode fiber; chromatic exists in both.
Polarization mode dispersion is a third, random, mechanism in single-mode fiber.

bank.q: A 12 km link uses fiber with α = 0.5 dB/km and has two splices of 0.1 dB each. The launched power is 1 mW. Find the loss in dB and the received power in dBm and in mW.
outline: Fiber loss = 0.5 × 12 = 6 dB; splice loss = 0.2 dB; total 6.2 dB.
1 mW is 0 dBm, so received power = 0 − 6.2 = −6.2 dBm.
State that losses in dB add directly, which is why the dB scale is used.

bank.q: A step-index multimode fiber has n₁ = 1.48, Δ = 0.01, core radius 50 μm and length 1 km. Estimate the pulse broadening from intermodal dispersion and the maximum bit rate the fiber could support.
outline: Use ΔT/L = n₁Δ/c.
Substitute: 1.48 × 0.01 / (3 × 10⁸) ≈ 4.9 × 10⁻¹¹ s/m, i.e. about 49 ns over 1 km.
State that the spread grows linearly with length.
Bit-rate estimate from ΔT ≤ 1/B gives roughly 20 Mbit/s for 1 km; note the estimate is order-of-magnitude.
Repeat for a graded-index fiber with optimum α to show n₁Δ²/(8c) gives about 62 ps/km.

bank.q: A standard single-mode link is 80 km long at 1550 nm with D = 17 ps/(nm·km). The source has a spectral width of 1 nm. Find the pulse broadening and compare it with a 10 Gbit/s bit slot.
outline: Bit slot at 10 Gbit/s is 100 ps, so the spread is more than ten bit slots; the link needs dispersion compensation or a narrower source.
Comment that Δλ for a DFB laser is well under 0.1 nm, which reduces ΔT by the same factor.
Note that D falls to zero at the zero-dispersion wavelength near 1310 nm.

bank.q: A fiber has a PMD coefficient of 0.5 ps/√km. Find the mean differential group delay over 100 km and judge whether it is acceptable at 10 Gbit/s.
outline: Mean DGD = 0.5 × √100 = 5 ps.
Bit slot at 10 Gbit/s is 100 ps; the usual design rule keeps mean DGD below about one tenth of the bit slot, i.e. 10 ps here, so the link passes.
Emphasize the √L law: quadrupling length doubles the delay, not quadruples it.
Mention that PMD is a random quantity, so the mean and the tail statistics both matter.

bank.q: A 100 km span of standard fiber has D = +17 ps/(nm·km). Find the length of dispersion-compensating fiber with D = −100 ps/(nm·km) needed to cancel the dispersion, and comment on the added loss if the DCF has 0.5 dB/km.
outline: Condition D₁L₁ + D₂L₂ = 0, so L₂ = 17 × 100 / 100 = 17 km.
The compensating fiber adds 17 × 0.5 = 8.5 dB of loss, which must be paid for with an amplifier or a stronger transmitter.
Also mention that DCF has a negative dispersion slope that must roughly match the link slope.
Alternative: use dispersion-shifted or non-zero-dispersion fiber, or electronic compensation.

bank.q: Compare pulse broadening in multimode step-index and multimode graded-index fibers. Why does the graded profile reduce the spread so strongly?
outline: Step index: all modes see the same index, so path length alone sets the delay; ΔT/L = n₁Δ/c, about 50 ns/km for Δ = 0.01.
Graded index: rays that swing far from the axis travel through lower-index glass, so their higher speed partly cancels their longer path.
With the near-parabolic profile (α ≈ 2), ΔT/L ≈ n₁Δ²/(8c); the ratio to the step-index case is Δ/8.
Numbers for Δ = 0.01: about 50 ns/km falls to about 60 ps/km.
Practical limits: profile errors, mode mixing and the difficulty of holding α near 2 across the core.

bank.q: Why is 1550 nm the preferred window for long-haul links even though the zero-dispersion wavelength is near 1310 nm? Discuss how the loss–dispersion trade-off is resolved.
outline: Loss: Rayleigh scattering falls as 1/λ⁴, giving about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm against 0.35 dB/km at 1310 nm; the infrared absorption tail sets the upper limit.
Dispersion: standard fiber has D ≈ +17 ps/(nm·km) at 1550 nm but nearly zero at 1310 nm.
Erbium-doped fiber amplifiers work in the 1530–1565 nm band, which favours 1550 nm.
Resolution: dispersion-shifted fiber moving the zero to 1550 nm, non-zero-dispersion fiber, dispersion-compensating fiber, or electronic compensation.
Note the four-wave-mixing penalty that pure dispersion-shifted fiber suffers in WDM systems.
Conclude that the loss saving of roughly 0.15 dB/km over 100 km (15 dB) outweighs the need to manage dispersion.

bank.q: Explain stimulated Brillouin and stimulated Raman scattering. Compare their thresholds, directions and shifts, and state how each affects a WDM link.
outline: Both are inelastic scattering processes in which a pump photon gives energy to a shifted wave; they become stimulated above a threshold power.
Brillouin: backward, shift about 11 GHz at 1550 nm, narrow gain bandwidth, threshold of a few milliwatts; P_th ≈ 21A_eff/(g_B L_eff).
Raman: forward, shift about 13 THz, broad gain band, threshold in the hundreds of milliwatts; the gain is used in distributed Raman amplifiers.
Effects on a link: SBS clips the launched power and causes back-reflection; SRS transfers power between WDM channels (channel crosstalk) at high total power.
Mitigations: keep power below threshold, widen the source linewidth to raise the SBS threshold, use large effective area fiber, space channels to limit Raman crosstalk.

glossary.def: The fall of optical power with distance along a fiber, quoted as a coefficient in dB per kilometre.
A logarithmic power ratio, 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁), used so that cascaded losses add instead of multiply.
An absolute power level referred to 1 mW, so 0 dBm = 1 mW and −3 dBm ≈ 0.5 mW.
A wavelength band where fiber loss is low, notably around 850 nm, 1310 nm and 1550 nm.
Absorption caused by the silica network itself, through ultraviolet electronic transitions and infrared vibrational transitions.
Absorption caused by impurities in the glass, chiefly OH⁻ ions and transition-metal ions.
A strong absorption band of the hydroxyl ion near 1380 nm, with weaker peaks near 950 nm and 1240 nm.
Fiber drawn from a dried preform so that the 1380 nm OH⁻ peak is reduced and the whole 1300–1600 nm range is usable.
Scattering from density fluctuations much smaller than the wavelength, with loss proportional to 1/λ⁴.
Scattering from defects or bubbles comparable to the wavelength, with a much weaker wavelength dependence than Rayleigh scattering.
Loss caused by curving the whole fiber to a small radius, so the field on the outside of the bend radiates away.
Loss caused by small random kinks along the fiber axis, usually from cabling or coating stress.
The bend radius below which bending loss rises sharply, roughly 3n₁²λ/(4π(n₁² − n₂²)^{3/2}).
One field pattern that can travel along the fiber, with its own propagation constant and group velocity.
Pulse spreading in multimode fiber because different modes take different paths and arrive at different times.
Multimode fiber whose core index decreases smoothly from the axis, equalising modal delays.
Pulse spreading because the group velocity depends on wavelength; measured in ps/(nm·km).
The part of chromatic dispersion coming from the wavelength dependence of the glass refractive index.
The part of chromatic dispersion coming from the way the mode's propagation constant depends on wavelength in a given core geometry.
The wavelength at which material and waveguide dispersion cancel; about 1310 nm for standard single-mode fiber.
Random delay between the two polarization modes of a real, slightly non-circular fiber; grows as the square root of length.
The arrival-time difference between the two polarization modes, in picoseconds.
Fiber designed so that its zero-dispersion wavelength falls at 1550 nm, in the lowest-loss window.
Fiber with large negative dispersion, spliced in to cancel the accumulated positive dispersion of a link.
The area A_eff over which the mode intensity is effectively spread; it sets the power density and hence the nonlinear thresholds.
Backward inelastic scattering above a few milliwatts, with a shift of about 11 GHz at 1550 nm.
Forward inelastic scattering with a shift of about 13 THz, useful for amplification but harmful as channel crosstalk.
